Instead of walking around without a plan, she went to the information desk near the main entrance. A student volunteer showed her the correct building and explained that Room 204 was on the second floor. Mei repeated the directions in English: enter the building, turn left, and take the stairs. She then found the classroom with fifteen minutes to spare. Before sitting down, she took a photo of the floor guide for later use. reading.title: A Realistic Weekly Schedule
reading.level: 基础衔接 · 原创模拟
reading.passage: Kai used to write a long list of tasks every morning. The list looked impressive, but he rarely finished it. He often put easy jobs first and left important work until late at night. This week, he tried a different method. On Sunday evening, he checked all his deadlines and chose three priorities for each day. He also estimated how much time each task would need. Instead of planning three hours without a pause, he divided the time into shorter periods and added small breaks. When an unexpected meeting took thirty minutes, he moved one low-priority task to another day rather than giving up the whole schedule. By Friday, Kai had not completed everything, but he had finished every urgent task. He learned that a useful schedule should guide decisions, not make a student feel guilty whenever a plan changes.

reading.titleZh: 不只看第一条搜索结果
reading.level: 基础衔接 · 原创模拟
reading.passage: For a class project, Olivia needed information about how city trees reduce summer heat. Her first online search produced thousands of results. She almost copied a statement from the first page, but the page did not name its writer or explain where the numbers came from. Olivia then used the university library database. She found a recent article written by environmental researchers and checked its list of sources. The article was harder to read, so she first studied the title, headings, and charts. She wrote the main idea in simple words and saved the full source information beside her note. Later, she compared the article with a report from the city government. The two sources used different examples but reached a similar conclusion. Olivia did not become an expert in one afternoon, yet she learned an important habit: useful research depends on checking who produced information and what evidence supports it.

reading.passage: During the first week of term, Chen often studied until one in the morning. He believed that more time at his desk would always produce better results. reading.passage: When Hana first joined an online course, she watched every video from beginning to end but remembered little. She usually kept several message windows open and sometimes answered friends while the teacher was explaining a key idea. Later, Hana changed how she used the platform. Before each lesson, she downloaded the worksheet and wrote two questions about the topic. During the video, she paused after each short section and answered one question without looking at her notes. She also placed her phone behind her laptop and turned off computer notifications for thirty minutes. If an explanation remained unclear, she marked the exact time instead of replaying the entire video. At the end, she wrote a three-sentence summary and uploaded it with her worksheet. The course did not become easier overnight, but Hana became a more active learner. Technology helped most when she used it to practise, not simply to keep information playing on a screen.

reading.title: A Reading Day for Children
reading.level: 基础衔接 · 原创模拟
reading.passage: The university reading club planned a Saturday event for children in a nearby community. At the first meeting, everyone suggested activities, but nobody recorded who would do each job. Two days later, the club leader noticed that three students were preparing the same game while no one had contacted the community center. The group met again and made a simple responsibility chart. Jia called the center, Omar selected short stories, and two other members prepared pictures and name cards. On Saturday morning, one volunteer was ill, so Omar welcomed families as well as leading a story group. Because the jobs were clear, other members could adjust without confusion. After the event, parents said their children had enjoyed talking about the stories. The volunteers also wrote down what should change next time. They learned that cooperation is not only sharing ideas; it also means accepting a clear responsibility and communicating when a plan changes.

reading.title: Looking Beyond the Lowest Price

reading.passage: Nadia needed a new water bottle for university. In a shop, she found a cheap plastic bottle and a metal bottle that cost almost three times as much. At first, the plastic one seemed like the obvious choice. Then Nadia compared more than the price. The metal bottle could be repaired with a new lid, while the plastic one would probably be thrown away if it broke. She also read instructions about cleaning and checked whether both products were safe for hot drinks. Nadia chose the metal bottle because she expected to use it for several years. Her decision does not mean that the most expensive product is always best. A high price can reflect advertising rather than quality. Nadia's method was to consider how often she would use an item, how long it might last, and what would happen at the end of its life. By asking these questions, shoppers can reduce waste without buying unnecessary “green” products.

reading.title: Preparing for a Campus Job Interview
reading.level: 基础衔接 · 原创模拟
reading.passage: Sofia saw an advertisement for a part-time assistant at the campus sports center. The hours fitted her class schedule, but she had never had a formal job interview. She first read the advertisement again and underlined three requirements: answering visitors' questions, keeping simple records, and working on Saturday mornings. Instead of memorizing a long speech, Sofia prepared short examples. To show communication skills, she described how she had explained club rules to new members. To show responsibility, she talked about arriving early for a volunteer event. She also wrote two questions for the employer about training and weekly hours. During the interview, Sofia did not understand one question immediately. She politely asked the interviewer to repeat it, then answered clearly. This moment did not make her look weak; it showed that she could solve a communication problem calmly. Sofia received the position, but the most useful result was learning to connect each job requirement with real evidence from her own experience.

reading.passage: During an international student dinner, Evan noticed that his classmate Aiko did not open a gift immediately. In Evan's family, people usually open gifts in front of the giver, so he first wondered whether Aiko disliked it. Instead of remaining silent, he asked politely if gift opening was different in her family. Aiko explained that she often waited until later because opening a gift slowly at home allowed her to show careful attention. She then asked about Evan's custom, and both students laughed at how easily they could have misunderstood each other. The conversation did not prove that everyone from one country behaves in the same way. Family habits differ, and people may make individual choices. What mattered was their method: they described what they had noticed, asked without making an accusation, and listened to the answer. By clarifying an unfamiliar action, Evan and Aiko turned a possible misunderstanding into a useful exchange.

reading.title: From Notes to a Clear Summary
reading.passage: During her first weeks at university, Mei tried to write down every word in each lecture. Because she was always looking at her notebook, she sometimes missed the speaker's next point. A classmate suggested a different method. Before a lecture, Mei now reads the title and writes two questions about the topic. While listening, she records only key terms, examples, and words that show a change of idea, such as however or therefore. Within ten minutes after class, she adds any details she still remembers. She then closes the notebook and explains the lecture aloud in one minute. If she cannot explain a point, she checks that part of her notes or asks a classmate. This process takes less time than copying everything and helps Mei notice what she truly understands.

reading.title: Three Checks Before Sharing
reading.passage: For a class project, Arun found a surprising number in a short online post. He wanted to use it immediately because it supported his argument. His partner asked him to make three checks first. They looked for the author, but the post gave only a user name. They searched for the original report and discovered that the number came from a survey published eight years earlier. Finally, they compared the survey with a recent university study. The newer study described a different group of people and reached a less dramatic conclusion. Arun did not throw away the old source. Instead, he explained its date and limits, then used the newer evidence for his main claim. He learned that checking a source does not simply mean deciding whether it is good or bad; it means understanding exactly what the source can support.

reading.title: The Empty Final Slide
reading.titleZh: 空白的最后一页幻灯片
reading.passage: Four students were preparing a presentation about local transport. At their first meeting, they discussed many ideas but did not assign clear roles. Everyone assumed that someone else would design the final slide, which needed to summarize their suggestions. Two days before the deadline, the slide was still empty. Instead of blaming one another, the group listed every unfinished task. Nadia agreed to create the final slide, while Leo checked the data and Kim corrected the language. Their leader, Bo, changed the schedule so that they could review the complete presentation the next evening. They also began using a shared table with each task, its owner, and its deadline. The project was submitted on time. More importantly, the group learned that cooperation requires visible responsibilities, not simply friendly discussion.

reading.title: Why a Correct Answer Was Not Enough
reading.passage: At the end of a study week, Ms. Zhou gave her class four reading questions. Rui answered three correctly and wanted to record only the score. Ms. Zhou asked him to underline the sentence that supported each answer. Rui quickly found evidence for two questions, but he could not locate support for his third correct choice. He admitted that he had guessed it from a familiar word in the option. For the question he answered incorrectly, he had found the right paragraph but ignored the word not in the question. Rui changed his review table. It now has columns for his answer, the correct answer, the evidence sentence, and the reason for any mistake. The table takes several extra minutes to complete, yet it shows whether success came from understanding or luck and whether an error came from vocabulary, grammar, or careless reading.

reading.title: The Afternoon Energy Experiment
reading.passage: Every afternoon, Daria felt sleepy during her two o'clock class. She assumed that the subject was boring and began buying a large sweet drink before class. The drink made her feel active for a short time, but an hour later she was tired again. For one week, Daria kept a simple record of her sleep, meals, drinks, and concentration. She noticed that the worst afternoons usually followed nights of less than six hours of sleep or mornings when she skipped breakfast. The next week, she changed three things: she went to bed at a regular time, ate a small breakfast, and carried water. Her class did not become easier, yet she could follow the discussion for longer. Daria's experiment did not prove that one routine works for everyone. It did show her that blaming the subject had hidden several habits she could change.

reading.title: Listening Before Offering Help
reading.passage: A university volunteer club planned to teach older residents how to use shopping apps. The students prepared detailed slides and expected a large audience. At their first community meeting, however, only six people showed interest in the class. Instead of cancelling the project, the volunteers asked residents what kind of help they actually needed. Several people wanted to learn how to book hospital visits online, while others needed a simple printed guide to local bus routes. One resident also pointed out that some neighbors did not own smartphones. The club divided into two teams. One created a small digital-skills workshop, and the other collected useful telephone numbers and transport information for a paper guide. More residents participated in the revised program. The students learned that useful service begins with questions, because a solution designed without local voices may solve the wrong problem.

reading.titleZh: 可重复使用杯计划有效吗
reading.passage: A campus cafe offered a small discount to customers who brought reusable cups. After one month, the manager announced that the plan was a success because the cafe had given 600 discounts. A student environment group asked for more information. They found that several regular customers had used the discount many times, so 600 discounts did not mean 600 different people had changed their behavior. The group then counted all drinks sold during two similar weeks. Reusable cups were used for 18 percent of drinks before the plan and 27 percent afterward. This was a clear increase, but most drinks still came in disposable cups. The students recommended keeping the discount and placing a washing station near the cafe. They also suggested measuring the result again during a busier month. Their conclusion was positive but careful: the measure helped, although there was room for further improvement.

reading.title: What a Screen-Time Number Cannot Tell You
reading.titleZh: 屏幕时长数字没有告诉你的事
reading.passage: When Anya saw that she spent more than six hours a day on screens, she decided that all digital activity was harmful. She set a two-hour limit, but soon broke it because her classes required online readings, group messages, and video lessons. Instead of abandoning the limit completely, she examined how she used each device. She divided screen time into planned study, necessary communication, and unplanned browsing. The total number of hours changed very little during the next week, yet unplanned browsing fell by nearly half. Anya achieved this by turning off social notifications during study sessions and writing one goal before opening her laptop. She also took short breaks away from the screen. Her record taught her that a single total can hide important differences. For her, the better question was not simply how long she used a screen, but whether each period of use matched a clear purpose.

reading.passage: Jun applied for several internships but received no interview invitations. His resume said that he was responsible, cooperative, and good at solving problems. He replaced “good at teamwork” with a short description of a class project in which he organized a shared schedule and helped the group meet its deadline. For problem-solving, he described how he noticed an error in survey data, checked the original forms, and corrected the report before submission. He also adjusted each application to match the skills named in the internship notice. A month later, Jun received two interview invitations. reading.passage: A university introduced an evening shuttle between the main campus and the nearest train station. The goal was to give students a safer alternative to walking and to reduce short car trips. During the first month, passenger numbers were high from Monday to Thursday but much lower on Friday and Saturday. A survey showed that most users valued the direct route and low price. However, students with late laboratory sessions complained that the final bus left twenty minutes too early. Nearby residents raised a different concern: empty buses sometimes waited with their engines running, creating noise and emissions. The university decided not to call the trial either a success or a failure. It added a later bus on two weekdays, reduced the weekend schedule, and instructed drivers to switch off engines while waiting. A second review will compare passenger numbers, costs, and complaints. The case shows that transport decisions often require several measures, not one simple total.

reading.titleZh: 讲述同一个故事的两种方式
reading.passage:
A class visited a local history museum on Saturday. Before entering, each student received a question sheet. One question asked why families had moved from nearby villages to the town a century earlier. The display did not repeat the words on the sheet. Instead, it explained that new factories offered regular wages, while farm work depended heavily on the season.

Several students chose the answer about better weather because they had noticed a picture of a sunny street. Others compared the options with the explanation and selected employment. After the visit, the teacher asked everyone to underline the evidence for their answer. She did not ask them to copy the whole display.

The exercise showed that finding a familiar word is not always enough. A picture may attract attention without explaining a cause. Readers need to connect ideas expressed in different words and check whether their evidence actually answers the question. Even a correct choice is worth reviewing if it was only a guess.
reading.passageZh:
一个班星期六参观了一家地方历史博物馆。进馆前，每位学生都拿到了一张问题单。其中一题问，一百年前附近村庄的家庭为什么搬到镇上。展板没有重复题目中的措辞，而是解释说，新工厂提供固定工资，而农业劳动高度依赖季节。

几名学生注意到一张阳光下街道的图片，便选择了“天气更好”的答案。其他人把选项与说明对照后，选择了就业。参观结束后，老师要求每个人画出支持答案的依据，而不是抄下整块展板。

这项练习说明，找到熟悉的单词并不总是足够。图片可能吸引注意，却没有解释原因。读者需要把不同措辞表达的意思联系起来，并检查证据是否真正回答了问题。即使选对了，如果只是猜的，也值得复盘。

reading.title: Read the Update, Not Just the Invitation
reading.titleZh: 不仅要读邀请，还要读更新通知
reading.passage:
A student signed up for a photography workshop after reading an invitation on a club page. The invitation listed a morning session in the art building and asked everyone to bring a camera. Two days before the workshop, the club sent an update. Repairs had made the original room unavailable, so the session would take place in the library that afternoon. Students could borrow cameras there.

The student noticed the familiar workshop title and closed the message without reading further. On the day, she arrived at the art building early and found a locked door. After calling a friend, she checked the update and changed her plan.

Later, the club made its messages clearer by placing changes at the top. It also kept the original invitation online, but added a link to the latest information. Clear communication requires effort from both sides: organizers should make important changes easy to notice, while readers should check whether their earlier understanding is still correct.
reading.passageZh:
一名学生看了社团网页上的邀请后，报名参加摄影工作坊。邀请上写着活动上午在艺术楼举行，并要求每人带相机。活动前两天，社团发来了更新通知。维修导致原教室无法使用，因此活动改到当天下午在图书馆举行。学生可以在那里借相机。

这名学生注意到熟悉的活动标题，没有继续往下读就关掉了消息。活动当天，她早早来到艺术楼，却发现门锁着。给朋友打电话后，她查看了更新通知，改变了计划。

后来，社团把变更放在消息开头，使通知更加清楚。它也保留了网上的原邀请，但添加了通向最新信息的链接。清楚的沟通需要双方努力：组织者应让重要变更容易被发现，读者也应检查自己先前的理解是否仍然正确。

reading.title: A Fair Share Is Not Always the Same Task
reading.titleZh: 公平分工不等于人人做同一件事
reading.passage:
Four students were preparing a poster for a campus exhibition. At their first meeting, they divided the work into four equal parts. Each person would collect facts, write a paragraph, and design part of the poster. The plan looked fair, but one member had little experience with design, while another could only work at the weekend.

During a second meeting, a quiet student explained why she had missed the first deadline. Instead of treating her silence as agreement, the others asked about her available time. They then assigned different roles. One checked the facts, another prepared pictures, and two wrote and edited the text. Everyone still checked the final poster together.

The group learned that fair cooperation requires more than identical tasks. Members need to discuss their skills and limits openly. Listening to a concern early can prevent a larger problem later, without removing anyone's responsibility.
reading.passageZh:
四名学生正在为校园展览制作一张海报。在第一次会议上，他们把工作平均分成了四份。每个人都要搜集事实、写一段文字并设计海报的一部分。这个计划看似公平，但一名成员缺少设计经验，另一名成员只能在周末工作。

第二次会议上，一名平时安静的学生解释了自己为什么没能在第一个截止日期前完成工作。其他人没有再把她的沉默当作同意，而是询问了她的可用时间。随后，他们分配了不同的职责：一人核对事实，一人准备图片，两人撰写并编辑文字。每个人仍然一起检查了最终的海报。

小组认识到，公平合作需要的不只是相同的任务。成员需要坦率讨论自己的技能和限制。尽早听取担忧可以避免日后出现更大的问题，同时不免除任何人的责任。

reading.title: The Price Beyond the Label
reading.level: 四级衔接专项 · 原创模拟（非真题、非新闻）
reading.topic: 理性消费与总成本比较
reading.passage:
Lin needed a desk lamp for her shared room. An advertisement offered a large discount on a familiar brand, and she almost made the purchase immediately. Before paying, however, she checked whether the lamp was suitable for her desk. It was too wide, and its special replacement bulbs were expensive.

A second lamp cost fifteen yuan more, but it used ordinary bulbs and fitted the space. Lin compared the purchase price with the likely cost of bulbs over two years. She also asked how much a simple repair would cost. This helped her see that the cheaper label did not necessarily mean a lower total expense.

Lin chose the second lamp and kept the receipt in a folder. Her decision was based on her needs and budget, rather than the size of the discount. A careful consumer does not always buy the cheapest item. Sometimes a slightly higher price is worth paying for a product that remains practical over time.
reading.passageZh:
林需要为自己合住的房间买一盏台灯。一则广告表示，一个她熟悉的品牌有大幅折扣，她差点立即购买。不过，付款前，她检查了这盏灯是否适合自己的书桌。灯太宽了，而且更换用的专用灯泡价格很高。

第二盏灯贵十五元，但它使用普通灯泡，尺寸也适合那个空间。林把购买价格和未来两年可能花在灯泡上的费用放在一起比较。她还询问了一次简单维修要多少钱。这让她认识到，标价较低未必意味着总开支更少。

林选了第二盏灯，并把购物小票放进文件夹。她的决定依据的是自己的需要和预算，而不是折扣大小。谨慎的消费者并不总是购买最便宜的物品。有时，为了得到一件长期保持实用的产品，多付一点钱是值得的。

reading.title: What Did the Cooler Number Mean?
reading.titleZh: 较低的温度数字说明了什么？
reading.level: 四级衔接专项 · 原创模拟（非真题、非新闻）
reading.topic: 城市树荫、测量条件与结论边界
reading.passage:
Mei joined a school project about trees and summer heat. Her group measured the road surface under a tree and in direct sunlight at noon. The shaded surface was eight degrees cooler. Excited by the result, Mei wrote that trees could lower the whole city's air temperature by eight degrees.

Her teacher asked what the device had actually measured. Mei checked her notes: it recorded surface temperature, not air temperature. The group had also visited only one street on one day. Its evidence could describe those two spots, but could not support a claim about the entire city.

The students changed their report and added the time, location and measurement method. They planned to compare more streets under similar weather conditions. Mei still believed urban trees were valuable. However, she now understood that a useful conclusion must match the evidence. A smaller, accurate claim can teach people more than a dramatic statement that the study does not support.
reading.passageZh:
梅参加了一个关于树木与夏季高温的学校项目。她的小组在中午测量了一棵树下和阳光直射处的路面温度。有树荫处的地表温度低八度。梅对这一结果很兴奋，于是写道，树木能让整座城市的空气温度降低八度。

老师问她，设备实际上测量的是什么。梅检查了笔记：设备记录的是地表温度，而非空气温度。小组也只在一天里走访了一条街。他们的证据可以描述那两个地点，却不足以支持关于整座城市的说法。

学生们修改了报告，补充了时间、地点和测量方法。他们计划在相似天气条件下比较更多街道。梅仍然认为城市树木很有价值。不过，她现在明白，有用的结论必须与证据相符。一个范围较小而准确的结论，比研究无法支持的夸张说法更能让人学到东西。

reading.title: A Label That Admitted What Was Unknown
reading.titleZh: 一张承认未知之处的展品说明
reading.level: 四级专项衔接 · 原创模拟（非真题、非新闻）
reading.topic: 博物馆展品说明、事实与推测
reading.passage:
During a visit to a local museum, Nora stopped beside a wooden box. Its label said that a farming family may have used it to keep important papers. Nora wondered why the museum did not simply name the family.

The guide explained that the box had been found in an old house. A photograph showed a similar box, but no name appeared on either object. Staff had checked records and interviewed local people. They could describe where the box was discovered, but they could not identify its original owner.

At first, Nora thought the uncertain label made the exhibition less useful. Then the guide asked her to compare two statements: the box was found in that house, and it belonged to a particular family. The first was supported by a written record; the second was only a possibility.

Nora changed her mind. An honest exhibition did not need a complete story for every object. By separating facts from guesses, the museum allowed visitors to understand both the evidence and its limits. A clear question could be as valuable as a confident answer.
reading.passageZh:
参观一家地方博物馆时，诺拉在一个木箱旁停下来。展品说明写道，一个农民家庭可能曾用它保存重要文件。诺拉想知道，为什么博物馆不直接写出这个家庭的名字。

导览员解释说，这个箱子是在一所老房子里发现的。一张照片上出现了一个相似的箱子，但这两件物品上都没有名字。工作人员查阅了记录，也采访了当地人。他们能够说明箱子在哪里被发现，却无法确认它最初的主人。

起初，诺拉觉得这张带有不确定表述的说明降低了展览的价值。随后，导览员请她比较两个说法：箱子是在那所房子里发现的；箱子属于某个特定家庭。第一个说法有书面记录支持，第二个却只是一种可能性。

诺拉改变了想法。诚实的展览不需要为每件物品都编出完整故事。通过区分事实与猜测，博物馆让参观者既了解证据，也了解它的局限。一个清楚的问题，可能和一个笃定的答案同样有价值。

questions.prompt: Why did Nora question the label at first?
questions.promptZh: 诺拉起初为什么对展品说明产生疑问？
options: It gave the wrong date for the photograph.
It named too many possible owners.
It did not state exactly which family had owned the box.
It said the box had never been used.
optionsZh: 它把照片的日期写错了。
它列出了太多可能的主人。
它没有明确说明哪个家庭曾拥有这个箱子。
它说这个箱子从未被使用过。
questions.explanation: 第一段最后一句说，Nora想知道为何博物馆不直接name the family。她质疑的是主人的身份没有确定，而非日期或使用情况。

questions.prompt: Which statement was supported by a written record?
questions.promptZh: 哪个说法有书面记录支持？
options: The box was discovered in the old house.
A named farming family made the box.
The box in the photograph was certainly the same object.
The original owner left a name inside the box.
optionsZh: 箱子是在那所老房子里发现的。
一个有明确姓名的农民家庭制作了箱子。
照片中的箱子确定就是同一件物品。
最初的主人在箱内留下了名字。
questions.explanation: 第三段明确把发现地点与归属某家庭对比，并说明前者有书面记录支持。similar只表示相似，不能推出照片中必然是同一物品。

questions.prompt: What does “the second” in the third paragraph refer to?
questions.promptZh: 第三段中的“the second（第二个）”指什么？
options: The second photograph found in the house
The second interview with a local resident
The possibility that the box contained a written record
The statement that the box belonged to a particular family
optionsZh: 在房子里发现的第二张照片
对一名当地居民的第二次采访
箱子里装着书面记录的可能性
箱子属于某个特定家庭的说法
questions.explanation: two statements之后依次列出发现地点和归属家庭；the second回指后一个说法。不要把上文出现的record误当成箱内物品。

questions.prompt: What did Nora learn from the visit?
questions.promptZh: 诺拉从这次参观中学到了什么？
options: Museums should avoid showing objects with missing information.
Explaining the limits of evidence can make an exhibition more useful.
A confident answer is always better than an open question.
A photograph is enough to identify any object's owner.
optionsZh: 博物馆应避免展示信息不完整的物品。
解释证据的局限可以让展览更有价值。
笃定的答案总比开放的问题好。
一张照片足以确认任何物品的主人。
questions.explanation: 最后一段通过Nora改变想法总结主旨：诚实区分事实和猜测能帮助参观者理解证据及其边界，不需要为每件展品强行给出完整故事。

listening.title: Instructions for the Museum Visit
listening.level: 四级专项衔接 · 原创模拟通知 · 合成朗读
listening.tip: 先盲听确定集合时间、地点和活动，再记下禁止事项。特别注意nine forty-five与ten的区别，以及photographs允许但flash不允许的转折。第三遍按短段听写，随后选3段跟读。美式英语语音优先；这不是四级真题录音。
listening.passage: Good afternoon, everyone. Tomorrow's museum visit begins at ten, but meet outside the main gate at nine forty-five. Bring your student card for free admission. The guide will first introduce the local history exhibition. You may take photographs, but please turn off your flash. Do not touch the original objects, even if they look strong. Some materials are fragile. During the final activity, choose one object and write down one fact and one unanswered question about it. We will discuss your notes on the bus back to school.
listening.passageZh: 大家下午好。明天的博物馆参观十点开始，但请在九点四十五分到大门外集合。带上学生证以便免费入场。导览员将首先介绍地方历史展览。可以拍照，但请关闭闪光灯。即使原件看起来很结实，也不要触摸。有些材料很容易损坏。在最后的活动中，选择一件物品，写下关于它的一个事实和一个尚未解答的问题。我们将在返校的巴士上讨论你们的笔记。
dictation: Bring your student card for free admission.
You may take photographs, but please turn off your flash.
dictationZh: 带上学生证以便免费入场。
可以拍照，但请关闭闪光灯。

questions.prompt: When should students meet outside the main gate?
questions.promptZh: 学生们应该几点在大门外集合？
questions.explanation: 通知区分了visit begins at ten与meet ... at nine forty-five。题目问集合时间，不是参观开始时间，应选九点四十五分。

questions.prompt: What should students write during the final activity?
questions.promptZh: 学生们在最后的活动中应该写什么？
options: One fact and one unanswered question about an object
The names of every visitor in their group
A complete story about the original owner
Instructions for repairing a fragile object
optionsZh: 关于一件物品的一个事实和一个未解答的问题
小组中每位参观者的名字
关于原主人的完整故事
修复一件易损物品的步骤
questions.explanation: 结尾直接要求write down one fact and one unanswered question about it。任务强调证据和未知信息，不能自行编写主人的完整故事。

sent.text: The guide who showed us the wooden box explained that the records which the staff had examined did not identify its original owner.
sent.main: The guide explained that the records did not identify its original owner.
sent.translation: 向我们展示木箱的导览员解释说，工作人员查阅过的记录并没有确认木箱最初的主人。
sent.structure: 主句主语The guide，谓语explained，宾语为that引导的整个从句。who showed us the wooden box是修饰guide的定语从句。宾语从句的主语是the records，谓语为did not identify；which the staff had examined是修饰records的定语从句，which作examined的宾语。its original owner指木箱最初的主人。
sent.mainZh: 导览员解释说，记录没有确认它最初的主人。
sent.topic: 主句谓语、宾语从句与两层定语从句
grammar: showed属于who定语从句，不是主句谓语；主句核心是guide explained。
explained后的that引导宾语从句，不在该从句内作主语或宾语。which则作had examined的宾语。
过去完成时had examined表示查阅记录发生在解释之前；did not之后用动词原形identify，不能用identified。
sent.examTip: 先框定guide explained，再找records did not identify。把who和which引导的两段修饰分别括起来，特别保留否定词not，避免把“没有确认”读成“确认了”。

trans.source: 这家博物馆保护历史物品，让参观者能够了解当地人的生活。
trans.answer: This museum preserves historical objects so that visitors can learn about local people's lives.
trans.grammar: 主语This museum为单数，谓语preserve加-s。so that引导目的状语从句，can后接原形learn。historical修饰objects；local people's lives表示当地人的生活。
acceptedAnswers: This museum preserves historical objects so that visitors can learn about local people's lives.
The museum preserves historical objects to help visitors learn about the lives of local people.
trans.topic: 文化遗产保护与目的表达
trans.alternative: The museum preserves historical objects to help visitors learn about the lives of local people.

trans.source: 虽然我们知道这个箱子在哪里被发现，但我们仍不知道它最初属于谁。
trans.answer: Although we know where the box was found, we still do not know who it originally belonged to.
trans.grammar: although引导让步状语从句，主句通常不再加but。where the box was found与who it originally belonged to都是宾语从句，使用陈述语序。belong to不是被动语态，不能写成was belonged to。
acceptedAnswers: Although we know where the box was found, we still do not know who it originally belonged to.
We know where the box was discovered, but we still do not know who its original owner was.
trans.topic: 让步关系与宾语从句语序
trans.alternative: We know where the box was discovered, but we still do not know who its original owner was.

2026-10-07.title: 兼职培训：用具体反馈改进工作流程
2026-10-07.grammarTip: 先划掉who或that引导的定语从句，再找主句谓语；experienced和punctual作表语时需要be动词。副词修饰动作，如check carefully；yesterday等过去时间提示一般过去时。阅读时区分“工作更快”与“减少返工”，听力抓培训时间、携带物品和操作顺序。材料为原创分级模拟，不是真题或真实新闻。

reading.title: A Better Way to Check an Order
reading.level: 四级衔接专项 · 原创分级模拟（非真题、非新闻）
reading.topic: 兼职培训、具体反馈与工作效率
reading.passage:
When Alex started a part-time job at a small printing shop, he thought a good employee should finish every order as quickly as possible. During his first week, however, he printed several pages in the wrong size. The shop had to use extra paper and spend more time correcting the work.

His manager did not simply tell him to be more careful. She asked him to describe each step he had taken. Together, they found that he often began printing before checking the customer's written request. An experienced worker then showed him a short checking routine: read the request, confirm the size, and print one test page.

At first, this routine made each order slightly slower. By Friday, Alex was making fewer mistakes and rarely needed to print an order again. He wrote down one problem after each shift and asked for advice on it the next day.

Alex learned that useful feedback points to an action a worker can change. Improving efficiency does not always mean moving faster; sometimes it means preventing the same mistake from happening again.
reading.passageZh:
亚历克斯开始在一家小印刷店做兼职时，认为好员工应该尽可能快地完成每份订单。然而，在第一周，他把好几页纸印成了错误的尺寸。商店不得不额外用纸，并花更多时间纠正这项工作。

经理并没有只让他更加小心。她让他描述自己采取过的每一个步骤。他们一起发现，他经常在检查客户的书面要求之前就开始打印。随后，一名有经验的工人教了他一套简短的检查流程：读要求、确认尺寸、打印一页样张。

起初，这套流程让每份订单都稍慢一些。到了星期五，亚历克斯犯的错误变少了，很少再需要重印整份订单。每次下班后，他都会记下一个问题，第二天针对这个问题请教。

亚历克斯明白了，有用的反馈会指出一个员工能够改变的具体行动。提高效率并不总是意味着动作更快；有时候，它意味着避免再次犯同样的错误。

questions.prompt: What caused some of Alex's early mistakes?
questions.promptZh: 亚历克斯早期的一些错误是什么原因造成的？

He started printing before checking the written request.

他使用了另一家店的检查流程。

questions.prompt: What happened after Alex adopted the checking routine?

He immediately completed every order faster.
He no longer needed to read customers' requests.
He stopped asking other workers for advice.

他立刻更快地完成了每一份订单。
他不再需要阅读客户的要求。
他不再向其他工人请教。
questions.explanation: 第三段说明起初略慢，但到周五错误和重印都减少。B中的immediately与At first...slightly slower冲突；C、D均不符合原文。

questions.prompt: What is the main lesson of the passage?

速度是衡量工作质量唯一有用的标准。
具体反馈可以通过减少重复错误提高效率。
有经验的工人不需要检查订单。
questions.explanation: 全文通过查明原因、改变步骤和减少重印展示具体反馈的作用，末段直接总结效率不只来自速度，也来自避免重复错误。

listening.title: A Notice for New Employees
listening.level: 四级衔接短通知 · 原创模拟 · 浏览器合成朗读
listening.tip: 第一遍抓住通知目的；第二遍区分培训开始时间和提前到达时间，记录携带物品与请假截止时间。重点听first、then和This time，辨认先示范、后结对练习的顺序。朗读优先采用可用美式英语语音，不是真题录音。
listening.passage: Hello, everyone. Tomorrow's training for new employees will start at nine in Room Three. Please arrive ten minutes early, but do not begin using the equipment alone. An experienced worker will first show you how to check each order. Then you will practice in pairs and receive feedback on one completed task. Last week's group tried to work quickly and missed several labels. This time, accuracy comes before speed. Bring a notebook, not your own tools. If you cannot attend, call the office before five today so we can arrange another session.
listening.passageZh: 大家好。明天的新员工培训将在九点于三号房间开始。请提前十分钟到达，但不要独自开始使用设备。一名有经验的工人会先示范如何检查每一份订单。随后，你们将结对练习，并就一项完成的任务获得反馈。上周那组人力求工作迅速，却漏看了几个标签。这一次，准确性比速度更重要。请带笔记本，不要带自己的工具。如果无法参加，请在今天五点前给办公室打电话，以便我们安排另一场培训。

Bring a notebook, not your own tools.

请带笔记本，不要带自己的工具。

questions.prompt: What should employees do before the training begins at nine?
questions.promptZh: 员工在九点培训开始前应该做什么？

2026-10-08.title: 周测复盘：共享洗衣房的错峰试验
2026-10-08.grammarTip: 本周复盘不新增课程词，由系统安排40个复习或自选待学词。语法继续检查主句谓语、be加形容词、不可数名词和before加动名词；阅读先找事实，再判断结论是否超出证据。听力区分提前到达时间、允许迟到时间与预约时长。先独立作答，再订正，保留首次成绩。本文和题目均为原创分级模拟。

reading.title: A Quieter Time to Do the Washing
reading.titleZh: 在不那么拥挤的时段洗衣服
reading.level: 四级衔接周测 · 原创分级模拟（非真题、非新闻）
reading.topic: 共享设施、错峰安排与证据范围
reading.passage:
Students in one college hall often waited for washing machines on Sunday evenings. Some asked the college to buy more machines. Before making that decision, a student group recorded when the existing machines were used. They found long lines after dinner, but several machines stood empty in the early afternoon.

The group posted a simple chart showing the quieter hours. For one week, volunteers tried washing earlier and reported how long they waited. Their average wait fell from twenty minutes to eight. However, several students with afternoon jobs could not change their routine. One student also pointed out that the trial week was unusually dry, so fewer people might have washed heavy clothes.

The group did not claim that the chart had solved every problem. It recommended keeping the chart and collecting information for another month, including rainy weeks. If long waits continued, extra machines could still be necessary.

The trial showed that changing a routine can make better use of shared equipment. It also showed why a promising result should be checked under different conditions before it becomes the basis for an expensive decision.
reading.passageZh:
一栋大学宿舍楼里的学生经常在周日晚上排队等洗衣机。有些人要求学校增购机器。在作出这个决定之前，一个学生小组记录了现有机器的使用时段。他们发现晚饭后队伍很长，但下午较早时有几台机器闲着。

小组张贴了一张简单的图表，标明不那么拥挤的时段。在为期一周的试验里，志愿者尝试提前洗衣，并报告等待了多久。他们的平均等待时间从二十分钟降到了八分钟。然而，几名下午要工作的学生无法改变作息。一名学生还指出，试验的那一周异常干燥，因此洗厚重衣物的人可能较少。

小组没有声称图表解决了所有问题。它建议保留图表，并再收集一个月的信息，其中要包括多雨的星期。如果长时间等待的情况持续存在，增添机器可能仍然有必要。

这项试验表明，改变日常安排能够更好地利用共享设备。它也说明，一个令人鼓舞的结果，在成为昂贵决策的依据之前，为什么还应该在不同条件下接受检验。

questions.prompt: What did the student group discover before the trial?
questions.promptZh: 学生小组在试验前发现了什么？
options: All the washing machines needed repair.
Some machines were unused in the early afternoon.
Every student preferred to wash clothes after work.
optionsZh: 所有洗衣机都需要维修。
下午较早时有些机器没有被使用。
每名学生都更喜欢工作后洗衣。
questions.explanation: 第一段最后一句说several machines stood empty in the early afternoon，与B同义。长队集中在晚饭后，并不代表全天都缺机器。

questions.prompt: Why was the unusually dry weather mentioned?
questions.promptZh: 文章为什么提到异常干燥的天气？
options: To explain why the chart was damaged.
To show that students no longer needed clean clothes.
To prove that rain always causes machine faults.
To suggest another possible reason for the shorter wait.
optionsZh: 为了解释图表为什么损坏。
为了表明学生不再需要干净衣服。
为了证明下雨总会造成机器故障。
为了提出等待时间缩短的另一种可能原因。
questions.explanation: 第二段指出干燥天气可能使洗厚重衣物的人减少，因此等待缩短不一定完全由错峰图表造成。might表示可能，并非已证实的原因。

questions.prompt: What did the group recommend next?
questions.promptZh: 小组建议下一步做什么？
options: Keep the chart and collect more information in different weather.
Remove the chart because one week proved it useless.
Buy extra machines immediately without further checks.
Require every student to stop working in the afternoon.
optionsZh: 保留图表，并在不同天气下继续收集信息。
撤下图表，因为一周已证明它无用。
不再核查，立即购买更多机器。
要求每名学生停止下午的工作。
questions.explanation: 第三段建议keeping the chart并再收集一个月的信息，including rainy weeks。小组既没有立即否定图表，也没有立刻决定购买机器。

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
questions.promptZh: 下面哪一结论最符合文章中的证据？
options: A one-week trial is enough for every important decision.
Buying more equipment is never a useful solution.
A useful early result still needs checking under different conditions.
Students with jobs are responsible for all the waiting.
optionsZh: 一周试验足以支持每项重要决策。
增购设备永远不是有用的办法。
初步结果即使有用，仍需在不同条件下检验。
所有等待都由有工作的学生造成。
questions.explanation: 末段强调promising result应先在different conditions下检验。A、B使用绝对化表述；C保留了试验有帮助但证据有限的两层意思。

sent.main: The students found that the new chart was useful, although it did not remove every difficulty.

reading.title: What a Headline Leaves Out
reading.titleZh: 标题没有告诉你的部分
reading.level: 四级衔接专项 · 原创分级模拟（非真题、非真实研究）
reading.topic: 调查范围、来源核查与标题中的过度概括
reading.passage:
At a campus lecture, Mia saw a headline on the screen: Bright Rooms Make Every Student Learn Better. It seemed to offer a simple answer to a familiar problem. The speaker then showed the short article behind it and asked the audience to find the source of its claim.

The original survey involved twenty students from one evening class. They had been asked which of two rooms they preferred. Most chose the brighter room, but nobody had measured how much they learned. The headline had changed a report about preference into a claim about learning. It had also turned a small group into every student.

Mia first thought this meant surveys were useless. The speaker disagreed. The survey could still tell the college something about those students' opinions. The problem was not that the answers had no value, but that the headline promised more than the evidence supported.

Before leaving, Mia wrote three questions in her notebook: Who took part? What was actually measured? Does the conclusion match the result? She decided to use these questions before sharing another surprising headline with her friends.
reading.passageZh:
在一场校园讲座上，米娅看见屏幕上有个标题：“明亮的房间让每个学生学得更好。”它似乎为一个熟悉的问题提供了简单答案。随后，演讲者展示了标题背后的短文，请听众找到这一说法的来源。

原始调查涉及一个晚课班里的二十名学生。他们被问到两间教室中更喜欢哪一间。大多数人选择了较明亮的教室，但没有人测量他们学会了多少东西。标题把一份关于偏好的报告变成了关于学习效果的说法，也把一小群人变成了每个学生。

米娅起初以为这意味着调查毫无用处。演讲者并不同意。调查仍然能让学校了解这些学生的一些看法。问题不在于答案没有价值，而在于标题作出的承诺超出了证据所支持的范围。

离开前，米娅在笔记本上写了三个问题：谁参与了调查？实际测量了什么？结论与结果是否相符？她决定，下次向朋友转发令人惊讶的标题前，先用这些问题检查一下。

他们多常转发科学文章。
是否所有学生都需要上晚课。
questions.explanation: 第二段说学生被问到which of two rooms they preferred；文章同时明确说没有人测量他们学会了多少，因此不能选A。

questions.prompt: What was one problem with the headline?
questions.promptZh: 这个标题存在什么问题？
options: It described the rooms without mentioning their size.
It admitted that the survey had no participants.
It said students disliked both rooms equally.
It made a claim about all students from a small group's preferences.

它承认调查没有参与者。
它说学生同样不喜欢两间教室。
它根据一小群人的偏好对所有学生作出了断言。
questions.explanation: 第二段指出标题把preference变成learning，并把a small group变成every student。D同时抓住了范围扩大和结论过强的问题。

questions.prompt: How did the speaker view the survey itself?
questions.promptZh: 演讲者如何看待调查本身？
options: It had limited value for understanding those students' opinions.
It proved that every bright room improved learning.
It was useless because surveys can never provide information.
It should be treated as a controlled experiment.
optionsZh: 它对于了解这些学生的观点具有一定但有限的价值。
它证明每一间明亮的教室都能改善学习。
它毫无用处，因为调查永远不能提供信息。
它应该被视为受控实验。
questions.explanation: 第三段说调查仍能让学校了解those students' opinions；价值有明确范围，不能推广成所有人的学习效果。limited在此指范围有限，不是完全无用。

options: Share headlines without opening the articles.
Avoid reading any report that includes a survey.
Check participants, measurements, and conclusions before sharing a claim.
Assume that a popular headline must be accurate.
optionsZh: 不打开文章就转发标题。
避开所有包含调查的报告。
转发说法前检查参与者、测量内容和结论。
认为热门标题一定准确。
questions.explanation: 最后一段的三个问题对应Who took part、What was measured和Does the conclusion match；米娅明确决定转发前使用它们。

reading.title: A Familiar Name Is Not Enough
reading.level: 四级衔接专项 · 原创分级模拟
reading.topic: 公交改线、真实目的地与信息核对
reading.passage:
When a city changed two bus routes, a university volunteer named Ben helped visitors at a temporary information desk. Many passengers asked for the bus to Central Station. Ben first answered with a route number, but several people returned looking confused.

He soon learned that Central Station was not always their final destination. One tourist wanted a hotel near its north entrance. A student planned to catch a train at the south entrance. The two entrances were separated by a long tunnel, and the new buses stopped on different sides. Giving everyone the same answer could add an unnecessary walk, especially for someone carrying heavy luggage.

Ben changed his first question. Instead of asking which station people wanted, he asked what they needed to do there. He then showed them the correct side on a simple map and explained where to get off.

The new conversation took slightly longer, but fewer passengers returned. Ben did not memorize a separate answer for every possible trip. He learned to check the purpose behind a familiar place name. Accurate travel advice, he realized, begins with understanding the journey rather than recognizing one word.
reading.passageZh:
一座城市调整了两条公交线路后，一位名叫本的大学志愿者在临时咨询台帮助游客。许多乘客询问去中央车站的公共汽车。本起初直接告诉他们线路号码，但几个人困惑地返回了咨询台。

他很快发现，中央车站并不总是他们最终要去的地方。一名游客想去车站北入口附近的酒店，一名学生则打算在南入口乘坐火车。两个入口之间隔着一条长隧道，而调整后的公交车分别停在不同侧。给每个人相同的答案可能让他们多走不必要的路，尤其是带着沉重行李的人。

本改变了自己的第一个问题。他不再只问人们要去哪个车站，而是问他们到那里要做什么。随后，他在一张简单地图上指出正确的一侧，并说明应该在哪里下车。

新的对话稍微长了一些，但返回咨询台的乘客减少了。本没有为每种可能的行程单独背一个答案，而是学会核对熟悉地名背后的实际目的。他意识到，准确的出行建议始于理解整个行程，而不只是认出某个词。

reading.title: A Label That Leaves Room for Questions
reading.titleZh: 为提问留出空间的展品标签
reading.level: 四级衔接专项 · 原创分级模拟
reading.passage:
A small campus gallery noticed that visitors often read the labels beside paintings and then moved on without looking closely at the pictures. The labels contained dates, names, and long explanations of what each work meant. Some students said they felt there was one correct response to every painting.

The gallery tried a different approach in one room. Each new label gave a few verified facts and one open question. Beside a portrait, for example, it asked what the position of the hands might suggest. Visitors were invited to discuss their ideas, but guides reminded them to distinguish personal impressions from facts about the artist.

During the trial, visitors spent longer looking at the paintings and asked more questions. However, the gallery did not claim that shorter labels always produced better learning. Some visitors still wanted detailed background information, so the old explanations remained available in a booklet. The aim was to offer a starting point for observation, not to remove useful knowledge.
reading.passageZh:
一家小型校园美术馆发现，参观者常常读完画作旁的标签后就继续往前走，没有仔细看画。标签包含日期、姓名，以及关于每件作品含义的长篇解释。有些学生说，他们觉得每幅画都只有一种正确的回应。

美术馆在一个展室尝试了不同的方法。每张新标签提供少量经过核实的事实和一个开放问题。例如，一幅肖像画旁的问题是：画中双手的位置可能暗示什么？参观者受邀讨论自己的想法，但导览员提醒他们区分个人感受和关于艺术家的事实。

试验期间，参观者观看画作的时间更长，提出的问题也更多。不过，美术馆并没有声称更短的标签总能带来更好的学习效果。一些参观者仍想了解详细背景，因此旧版解释仍保留在一本小册子中。目的在于提供一个观察的起点，而不是删除有用的知识。
